# Key problems

16 problems, four per track, rephrased from the challenges each track lists on the sprint page. Ideas for each one are in [ideas.md](ideas.md). The interactive map is [mindmap/index.html](../mindmap/index.html).

## Track 1 · Model epistemics & decision evals

*Does a model know how solid its claims are, and can its confidence be elicited and checked?*

- **P1.1 Decision confidence vs. outcomes.** A model's confidence in its recommendations may not match how often they work out, and the outcomes that would show this arrive weeks or years later.
- **P1.2 Implied vs. defended claims.** What a model implies differs from what it will defend under questioning: it oversells, flip-flops and misstates its evidence.
- **P1.3 Honesty scores vs. decision quality.** We don't know whether models that rank higher on honesty benchmarks actually help people make better decisions.
- **P1.4 Benchmark decay and gaming.** Epistemic benchmarks leak into training data, saturate, and can be gamed with cheap tricks, so their rankings stop meaning anything.

## Track 2 · Trust infrastructure

*How do we make checking claims and tracing their origins cheap, routine and hard to manipulate, for people and for AI agents?*

- **P2.1 Gameable reliability scores.** Source-reliability scores can be gamed (cherry-picking easy claims, vague hedging, flooding with trivial truths) and are hard for outsiders to audit.
- **P2.2 No tamper-evident layer.** AI observability standards (the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions) record what agents did, but nothing makes those records tamper-evident.
- **P2.3 Do trust signals help?.** We don't know whether reliability and provenance signals (source scores, C2PA, Community Notes) make AI agents or people more accurate.
- **P2.4 How much is checkable?.** Nobody knows what share of a domain's content (council minutes, health advice, financial news) can be tied to checkable evidence.

## Track 3 · Epistemic products

*Do tools improve the decisions people endorse later, not just how satisfying the advice feels?*

- **P3.1 Satisfying vs. endorsed advice.** Advice that feels good in the moment (sycophancy) can lead to choices people later regret, and can deepen dependence on the assistant.
- **P3.2 Chatbots and disputes.** A chatbot helping one side of a conflict may escalate it, for example by validating grievances and drafting harsher messages.
- **P3.3 Briefings that miss what matters.** AI decision briefings may read well yet leave out the considerations that should drive the decision.
- **P3.4 Do cruxes change decisions?.** We don't know whether showing a group its cruxes, shared ground and inconsistencies changes what it decides.

## Track 4 · Open track

*What else advances AI for epistemics, including meta-questions about deployment, adoption and impact?*

- **P4.1 No unit of decision quality.** The field has no defensible unit for "decision quality improved", its equivalent of the QALY.
- **P4.2 Legislatures can't adopt AI tools.** Certification, budget and procurement rules keep official AI tools out of legislatures.
- **P4.3 Ignored forecasts.** Institutions often ignore forecasts they commissioned.
- **P4.4 Measuring live deployments.** It is hard to measure a live deployment's effect using only data you can download in a weekend.

## Cross-cutting themes

- **Late or missing ground truth.** Outcomes arrive weeks or years after the decision, or never. (P1.1, P3.1, P4.1, P4.3)
- **Goodhart and gaming.** Any score that matters gets optimized against, by models, sources or institutions. (P1.4, P2.1, P2.2, P3.3)
- **Warranted updating vs. caving.** Changing your mind for good evidence is a virtue; changing it for social pressure is sycophancy. (P1.2, P3.1, P3.2, P3.4)
- **Hindsight endorsement as the target.** The goal is decisions people stand behind later, not advice that feels good now. (P3.1, P3.3, P4.1)
- **Auditability.** A check only builds trust if outsiders can recompute it from public records. (P2.1, P2.2, P2.4, P4.4)
- **Are the signals used at all?.** Good signals are useless if agents, people and institutions ignore them. (P2.3, P4.2, P4.3)
